Self-audit pass over the bot review. No code change on this branch: the two correctness findings do not reproduce, and the remaining notes are coupling deltas.

**Already handled — a callee arriving with its own `+`/`-` sigil.** `_member_keys` strips one with `lstrip("+-")` before trying `-sel` then `+sel`, so a parked entry that already carries a sigil cannot ask the index for `--greet`. `test_an_objc_callee_that_already_carries_a_sigil_still_binds` pins it.

**Does not reproduce — `@protocol` nodes contradicting the documented exclusion.** Two separate mechanisms keep them out. `_resolve_objc_member_calls` excludes them explicitly via `_is_protocol_declaration` (the extractor labels a protocol `<Name>`), and the merge-side index cannot match one either: `cross_repo_calls._key()` preserves the angle brackets, so `<Greeter>` is never the key a parked receiver type `Greeter` looks up. The `_callable_class` marker the extractor now stamps on protocols is read by `_is_type_like_definition`, which is label-based and ignores it — the marker exists so protocols are visible to the passes that index declarations at all, exactly as a Java/C# interface is.

**On the coupling deltas** for `link_cross_repo_member_calls` and the two new tests: the fan-out is the shape of the pass, one small helper per decision (suffix family, member relations, member keys, key normalisation), and the tests fan out because each one builds two repos and merges them. Splitting either to move the metric would make both harder to read.

Investigated the latest bot findings on this PR (matching 38259c8).

Confirmed real, fixed in d8e6939:

1. A bracket span whose content contains a literal dot (e.g. [My.Table]) came out corrupted after rewriting to backtick form. Root cause is in tree_sitter_sql's own grammar, not this Python code: dumping the AST for the rewritten source shows the grammar splits `My.Table` into `My` (a malformed identifier with an empty closing backtick child), a bare `.` qualifier token, `Table`, and a dangling stray backtick landing in its own ERROR node. No amount of escaping on this end can round trip that. Fix: _debracket_tsql now refuses to rewrite a bracket span whose content holds a dot, leaving it as plain, un-rewritten bracket text (the same fallback behavior that existed before this PR).

2. _debracket_tsql's single and double quote scanning stopped at the first newline unconditionally, even when the string was not actually closed there. That meant a still-open multi-line string (dynamic SQL split across lines, say) had its later lines scanned as ordinary source, so bracket-like content on a later line got mistaken for a real identifier and rewritten, corrupting the string. Confirmed empirically: `_debracket_tsql(b"SET @sql = 'first line\n[NotAnIdentifier] second line';\n")` rewrote the bracket inside the still-open string. Fix: the scan now follows a quoted string to its real closing quote across newlines, matching how the engines actually read one. A string that genuinely never closes just consumes the rest of the file this way, which only means nothing past it gets debracketed, same as before this PR existed.

Both fixes have regression tests and are propagated through the whole stack (#2723/#2722/#2721/#2724).

Already covered by an earlier comment on this PR: the "numeric bracket identifiers not debracketed" finding (accepted, documented trade off) and the reproduced _scan_sql behavior claim (verified as a tooling artifact against unmodified upstream).

Follow up on the two remaining findings from the last bot review (matching 38259c8):

Confirmed real, fixed in ab1f115: a PostgreSQL dollar quoted PL/pgSQL body ($$ ... $$ or $tag$ ... $tag$) is opaque body text, not SQL to debracket, but _debracket_tsql had no handling for it at all. Bracket like text anywhere inside such a body (SELECT [NotReallyBracketIdent]; inside a function) was mistaken for a real bracket identifier and rewritten to backtick form, corrupting the body. Confirmed empirically before the fix, both for the untagged $$ and tagged $tag$ forms. Fix: the scan now skips a dollar quoted span whole, the same way it already skips a string or comment. Follow up on this round's bot finding (matching fe3b0b8):

Confirmed real, fixed: "Backtick escape not un-doubled when un-rewriting bracket identifiers". Traced this to the grammar, not the un-rewriting side: a T-SQL bracket identifier containing a literal backtick ([Foo\`Bar], a legal name since only ] needs escaping inside a bracket) gets escaped by doubling when rewritten to backtick form (\`Foo\`\`Bar\`, matching MySQL's own convention), but tree_sitter_sql's grammar treats the first backtick of that doubled pair as the closing delimiter rather than an escape -- confirmed via a direct AST dump, which showed the identifier truncated to \`Foo\` with \`Bar\` left behind as a separate ERROR node. _strip_backtick_parts's own un-doubling is actually correct; it just never receives correct input, since the grammar already mangled the parse before un-rewriting gets a chance to run. Same root cause and same fix as the earlier dot-in-brackets and native-backtick-identifier findings on this stack: _debracket_tsql now also refuses to rewrite a bracket span whose content contains a literal backtick, leaving it as plain bracket text. **Nullable builtin types parked as unresolved (extract.py:4476) — the premise does not hold.**
Nullability is unwrapped before the lookup: `_php_declared_type_name` strips `optional_type`, so

and only becomes an edge if a declaration of that name actually turns up in the merged corpus.
Adding a PHP stdlib class list would trade that for a new failure mode, since a project is free
to declare its own namespaced `DateTime`.

Still present in **0.9.55**, and here is a minimal repro that isolates the variable with a control document in the same run.

`build.py:41` is unchanged: `_AST_LOC_RE = re.compile(r"^L\d")` (still unanchored, so `L6220-L6260` matches too), and `watch.py:1994` still calls `to_json(..., force=True)`.

### Minimal repro

Three files, plus a hand-written `graph.json` whose doc nodes carry **no `_origin`** — the shape any graph built through the Claude Code skill has. The two documents differ **only** in the shape of `source_location`:

```
code.py             def alpha(): return 1
doc_lineloc.md      6 concept nodes, source_location "L10".."L15"
doc_sectionloc.md   6 concept nodes, source_location "§0".."§5"
```

```python
def sem(i, doc, loc):
    return {'id': f'{doc.replace(".","_")}_c{i}', 'label': f'{doc} concept {i}',
            'file_type': 'concept', 'source_file': doc, 'source_location': loc,
            'community': 0, 'community_name': 'Docs', 'norm_label': f'{doc} concept {i}'}

nodes  = [sem(i, 'doc_lineloc.md',    f'L{10+i}') for i in range(6)]
nodes += [sem(i, 'doc_sectionloc.md', f'§{i}')    for i in range(6)]
nodes += [{'id':'code_alpha','label':'alpha()','file_type':'code','source_file':'code.py',
           'source_location':'L1','community':1,'community_name':'Code',
           'norm_label':'alpha()','_origin':'ast'}]
```

Then append a function to `code.py` and run `graphify update .`:

```
doc_lineloc.md:    3 nodes total, 0/6 original concept nodes survived
doc_sectionloc.md: 6 nodes total, 6/6 original concept nodes survived
```

The line-located document's semantic layer is gone, replaced by 3 AST heading nodes. The section-located one is untouched. Same run, same absence of `_origin`, same file type — only the `source_location` shape differs.

### Real corpus, same run

Documentation repo, ~2.2k nodes, `graphify update .` after editing two unrelated `.md` files:

| source_file | `source_location` shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plans/2026-07-19-...md` | `L15`, `L6220-L6260` | 55 semantic | 0 semantic, 60 AST headings (`_origin: ast`, `file_type: document`) |
| `status/2026-07-20-...md` | `3`, `4.8` | 24 semantic | same 24, byte-identical |

Nothing surfaced the loss at the time. It came to light only on the next incremental `build_merge`, which reported edges whose endpoints pointed into that file and no longer resolved.

Two triage notes:

1. **The total went UP**, 2230 → 2243, because AST heading nodes outnumbered the semantic nodes they replaced. So even without the `force=True` on this path, the #479 guard would have passed — this is the exact masking [#2229](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/issues/2229) describes, with concrete numbers.
2. **The graph-health diagnostic stays clean** through the loss: 0 dangling, 0 missing, 0 collapsed. Consistent with what @1sraFigueroa reported on the `build_merge` side.

### On the fix

The `^L\d+$` anchor proposed above would not have saved this corpus on its own: `L15` is a bare integer and still matches. The `_origin` stamp (this issue's primary fix) and the strict-`_origin` check for fresh chunks are what actually cover it. The anchor is still worth having for citation spans like `L6220-L6260`.

Worth noting for reproduction: the skill's own extraction spec shows line references as valid `source_location` values, and the generated project `CLAUDE.md` instructs agents to run `graphify update .` after every edit — so on a doc-heavy corpus this fires on ordinary use, not on an exotic configuration.

Reproduced, and a fix has been put together. The diagnosis in the report is close, but the hot path isn't a linearity-unsafe regex. Every `re.sub` and every pattern in the extractor is linear. The `re` frames showing up in your `sample` output are the innermost frames of a quadratic *caller*, not the cause of it.

## Root cause

`_normalize_ts_import_types` in `graphify/extract.py` (the #3154 TypeScript `import(...)` type normalizer) filters regex matches against tree-sitter `type_arguments` byte ranges using a nested linear scan:

```python
matches = [m for m in matches
           if not any(start <= m.start() < end for start, end in original_type_ranges)]
```

The same shape is repeated in the second pass. The cost of that is O(matches x ranges). On top of it, `m.start()` gets re-evaluated inside `any()` once per range, which is why the profile ends up dominated by `re.Match.start` and the genexpr, and why `sample` attributes the time to `_sre`.

Both of those counts scale with file size in TS code that mixes generic calls (`fn<A, B>(x)`, which contributes one `type_arguments` range each) with `import(...)` types. The filter was measured in isolation, with everything else held constant:

| file | `import()` sites | `type_arguments` | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.8 MB | 10,000 | 10,000 | ~21 s | 0.003 s |
| 2.1 MB | 25,000 | 25,000 | ~2.6 min | 0.008 s |
| 4.2 MB | 50,000 | 50,000 | ~11.8 min | 0.019 s |

Every symptom in the report is accounted for by this:

- **100% CPU with zero open files.** All of the work happens in memory once the file has been read, so nothing is held open while it spins.
- **The freeze point shifting with the file set.** It gets triggered by content, meaning a handful of large generated or barrel `.ts` files, rather than by file count. Those live under `packages/`; your other top-level dirs and the 60-file repo don't contain any.
- **`--max-workers 1` stalling earlier (500/2469).** A single worker reaches the pathological file sooner, instead of ten workers racing past ~2400 first. The stall point isn't meaningful on its own.
- **Never completing.** With several such files in one tree the total runs into hours, so `graph.json` never gets written at all.
- **`--no-dedup`, `0.9.53` and `0.9.54` all reproducing.** The code sits in the extract path and is unchanged across those three releases, so none of those knobs can route around it.

## Fix

Both scans are replaced by a binary search over start-sorted ranges, combined with a prefix maximum of the `end` values, so a lookup only has to touch nesting depth rather than every range in the file. Type-argument ranges nest but never partially overlap, which is what makes the prefix max a correct stop condition. The subtle part is that an inner *closed* sibling must not be allowed to terminate the walk early.

Normalization behaviour itself is left untouched. Byte length and line count are still preserved, the same masking decisions are made, and the runtime-vs-type disambiguation from 6baa5e0 is kept exactly as is. The new lookup was checked against the old predicate with a 500,000-case differential test, including randomly generated non-nested ranges so the nesting assumption is exercised from both sides. No mismatches were found.

A regression test has been added as `test_ts_normalizer_scales_linearly_on_large_files`. It asserts on *scaling*, meaning that doubling the input must not roughly quadruple the time, rather than on wall clock, so it doesn't become machine dependent or flaky on slower CI boxes. On the current code it fails at 3.4x; after the change it passes.

One thing worth mentioning: `graphify-out/cache` shouldn't need to be kept around for this. The failure reproduces from the shape of the generated source alone, so a synthetic file is enough to see it.

Additional downstream evidence for this, from a ~10k-node repository graph (graphify 0.9.51):

**Measured silent divergence, 2026-09-05, six minutes after a rebuild:** `.graphify_analysis.json` referenced 34 nodes `graph.json` no longer contained, and 1,149 of 10,107 shared nodes carried a different community id between the two files. A tool reading both succeeded at 10:47 and raised `KeyError` at 10:52 — nothing could warn in between, because neither artifact records which clustering run produced it.

**Writer-set confirmation (matches this issue's analysis):** in our workflow the analysis sidecar is written only by `extract` and `cluster-only`/`label` — never by `update`, `watch`, or the git hooks — so for watch/update-driven workflows it is stale by construction.

**The fix may already be shipped in part:** `cluster.community_member_sigs` (sha256 over each community's sorted member ids) recomputes from `graph.json` and reproduced our shipped `.graphify_labels.json` `.sig` byte-identically (426/426 communities, algorithm stable v0.9.40→v0.9.54). Our ask matches this issue's direction: write that existing signature into **every** derived artifact on **every** write path (update/watch/hooks included), so downstream readers can verify two artifacts describe the same clustering — or refuse when they don't. We've adopted refuse-on-mismatch downstream; today it can only be done by recomputing against files the sidecar doesn't stamp.

```
extract.py:1370: error: Variable "graphify.extract._TsRangeIndex" is not valid as a type  [valid-type]
extract.py:1387: error: _TsRangeIndex? has no attribute "__iter__" (not iterable)  [attr-defined]

Independent confirmation from a large C# estate, plus one consequence of this bug that is not in
#3212 — and it is the one that hurt us.

**The `calls` edge does not land on the wrong node. It disappears.**

When the receiver of a member call is a **property**, the call gets no outgoing edge at all. A
**field** or a local variable in the same class still resolves. Two files, no corpus, no build
(`dotnet build` on net8.0: 0 errors, 0 warnings):

```csharp
// Service.cs
namespace Demo { public class Service { public void Do() { } } }

// Host.cs
namespace Demo
{
    public class Host
    {
        private Service Dependency { get; set; }   // property
        private Service _field;                    // field (control)

        public void A() { this.Dependency.Do(); }  // no edge
        public void B() { Dependency.Do(); }       // no edge
        public void C() { this._field.Do(); }      // edge
        public void D() { _field.Do(); }           // edge
        public void E() { Service s = new Service(); s.Do(); }  // edge
    }
}
```

`graphify extract src --code-only --no-cluster --out out`

| Version | edges of the 5 |
|---|---|
| v0.9.47 | 5 |
| v0.9.48 | 5 |
| **v0.9.49** | **3** |
| v0.9.50, v0.9.52, v0.9.55 | 3 |
| **v0.9.56** (released yesterday) | **3** |
| v0.9.55 + this PR | **5** |

So it starts at v0.9.49, the release that added the per-property member node, and this PR fixes it
completely. In the unpatched graph `.A()` and `.B()` have **no outgoing edge whatsoever** — nothing
is redirected to the property node, so the "edges arriving at a member" counter in #3212 does not
see this case at all. The property's declared type is still recorded into the method-scoped
receiver table on both sides of the change; that code is untouched. The only structural difference
in the reproducer is that the node for the property exists from v0.9.49 on.

**Measured impact.** ~15,300 `.cs` files across eight graphs (mixed .NET Framework and net8), both
versions built fresh from the same tree on the same day, compared over `(source_file, label)` after
excluding renamings and redirections:

* **383 `calls` edges lost** — present in the v0.9.39 extraction, absent in v0.9.55.
* **241 of them in a single graph** of the eight.
* Every one was read off the syntax tree at the call site, not sampled. The receivers are ordinary
  service properties reached through `this`; the six most frequent account for 85 of the 383
  (24, 21, 15, 9, 8 and 8 occurrences).

A property is the idiomatic way to hold an injected dependency, so the loss falls precisely on the
kind of edge a graph gets queried for. Post-processing cannot compensate: the edges are already
gone from the raw extraction.

**With the patch, a full portfolio rebuild is clean.** We also carry #2676; the two cherry-pick
onto `v8` @ `c9f9901` together without a conflict (auto-merge in `engine.py`). Full suite on
Windows: 17 failed / 5397 passed, and those 17 are the same by name on unpatched `v8` — all
platform-bound (`os.mkfifo` / `os.symlink` unavailable, `WinError 32` on `rmdir`, POSIX path and
install-destination assertions). Nothing in extraction. The `+14` passing over unpatched is exactly
the 9 tests here plus the 5 from #2676.

We run this patch in production locally, because without it v0.9.55 and later are not usable for
us. The reproducer above is the whole of it — two files, no corpus, and the version table is
reproducible from PyPI releases alone.

## Reply to the Graphify reviews

**First review (symlink / `6805542`)** — those findings were real. Fixed on `f976450`: every candidate goes through `_resolves_under_root` again (not only `islink()` files), and the memory walk prunes out-of-root symlink directories so `followlinks=True` cannot admit regular files from the target.

**Health / coupling** — expected. Git enumeration reuses `_is_noise_dir` so walk and `ls-files` prune the same trees. `detect()`’s caller count is pre-existing. Not splitting those helpers in this PR.

**Second review (`f976450`) — Worth a look**

1. **memory_dir files may be lost when git enumeration replaces all_files** — not a bug. After `git_enum` assigns `all_files`, we still merge `graphify-out/memory` via `_walk_from(..., in_memory=True, descend=True)` whenever that directory exists. Git usually never lists `graphify-out/` (gitignored); the extra walk is what keeps memory files. The `out_prefix`/`mem_prefix` filter only drops other `graphify-out/` paths if Git happened to list them.

2. **code_only skips Google Workspace/Office conversion but stores the original binary** — `code_only` here means “skip word-count / skip expensive conversion”, not “drop documents”. `test_detect_code_only_skips_word_count` still expects `.md` documents in the result. Office/Workspace names pass `_maybe_code_filename` because they are corpus extensions. Storing the original path without converting is the cheap path; extract cannot read those binaries as text. Skip-vs-convert for those types is a separate detect-policy change, not a git-enum bug.

3. **non-descend walk clears dirnames only when not in_memory** — not reachable. `_walk_from(..., descend=False)` is only used for the scan root (`in_memory=False`). The memory walk is always `descend=True`. `dirnames.clear()` is not used to stop a memory walk.

4. **Escaping .gitmodules path can make scanner run Git outside the scan root** — `git -C` may run on an overlapping ancestor when the scan root is a subfolder of a superproject. `_ingest_git_relpaths` drops any path that is not under the scan root. `_worktree_overlaps_scan` skips worktrees that neither contain nor are contained by the scan root, so a `path = /tmp/evil` gitmodules entry is not enumerated unless it actually overlaps. Admitted files cannot escape the scan root.

5. **Concurrent subtree walkers mutate shared `ignored_dirs`** — True-only memo. Duplicate `add` of the same `Path` is idempotent; a missed memo only repeats `_is_scan_ignored`. Walkers do not iterate the set. CPython’s GIL makes `set.add` / `in` atomic. A lock would not change scan results.

One extra data point that may be useful evidence for the "unrelated hub outranks a real match" case you describe, because it makes the inversion much larger than degree alone.

`_search_tokens` splits on punctuation and `_`, but not camelCase, so `handleTeamConfigWrite` stays **one** token. A natural-language query can therefore only reach it through the substring tier — 1/1000th of an exact match. For `"which worker route validates team config writes"`:

| node | query terms matched | score |
|---|---|---|
| `worker` — a local variable in a service worker | 1 of 6 | **126.0** |
| `handleTeamConfigWrite()` — the answer | 4 of 6 | **15.1** |

The coverage scaling from #1602 penalises a 1-of-6 match by 36×, but the exact/substring tier gap is 1000×, so a lone exact hit on a common word still wins by 8×. In that query the correct file sat at position 12.

So the hub problem your PR fixes has a scoring twin: even after the ordering is right, the score being ordered can be inverted for any identifier written in camelCase — which is most of them in TS/Java/Go/C#. #3417 adds a sub-word tier for that, and a plural fold so "writes" reaches `Write`.

Fourteenth round: one real fix, three disproved, and one finding that was right in a way that made me delete two of my own earlier commits' worth of logic.

**2018 bare use paths treated as external even when they name a local module** — correct, and it goes further than the finding says. I stopped reasoning about Rust from memory and asked rustc 1.96:

```rust
// edition 2021
pub mod models;
use models::Risk;        // compiles
```

Uniform paths, stable since 1.32, resolve a `use` path in the current module scope like any other path. Worse for my earlier reasoning, the shadowing case compiles too — a crate with both `src/anyhow.rs` and `anyhow` in `[dependencies]`, where `use anyhow::Result;` binds the **local** module (it type-checks against the local `struct Result`, which anyhow's generic `Result<T>` would not).

So the premise behind rounds ten and thirteen was simply false. The "local module shadows the dependency" failure those commits were built to prevent is Rust's own documented behavior, and the gate did nothing but drop real edges. Reverted in `85c1e74`, along with the whole edition-reading apparatus — which also dissolves this round's `_rust_package_edition inherits from probe.parent` finding, since the function no longer exists. Net −95 lines. Two tests pin the rustc-verified behavior instead of my assumption.

That also means round thirteen's workspace-inheritance fix, which I described as the most valuable thing in that round, was careful work on a function that should not have existed. My error, not the reviewer's.

Confirmed real, fixed (now at 5c677a9). Turns out this is a pre-existing tree_sitter_sql grammar limitation, independent of any rewriting this stack does -- confirmed by feeding a raw, untouched multi-part bracket reference straight to the parser with none of this module's code involved at all. This covers the realistic case: one dot-containing part combined with an otherwise normal 2-part reference, in either position.

Not fully fixed, and called out transparently: a rarer case where the dot-containing part's content is genuinely split across sibling AST nodes rather than merely having an extra bracket character (observed in a 3-part reference where the dot-part is the third segment, and in a pathological case with two adjacent dot-containing parts) still loses some content. Reconstructing the full name there would mean walking to and stitching together sibling ERROR node text, a meaningfully bigger change for a narrower, less realistic trigger. Below is my plan and a first-pass implementation sketch for review before I open the PR. ### Root cause (recap) `global_add` currently does a full load → prune → merge → cross-repo-resolve → save cycle **on every call**, and the CLI only ever calls it once per repo. That makes adding `K` repos sequentially `O(K²)`: ``` T(K) ≈ Σ(i=1..K) O(i) = O(K²) ``` The chart below is the sequential-vs-batched shape from the benchmark data already in this issue (5/10/20/40 repos): *(chart: sequential climbs from 1.67s → 89.52s across 5→40 repos; batched stays near-flat, 0.66s → 5.89s — ~15.2× faster at 40 repos)* ### Approach Add a batch entry point that loads once, applies every repo's prune+merge, resolves cross-repo links once, and saves once. Keep the existing single-repo `global_add` as a thin wrapper so nothing calling it today has to change. ```python # graphify/global_graph.py def global_add_many( graph_paths: list[Path], tags: list[str | None] | None = None, ) -> None: """Add/update multiple repo graphs in a single pass. One load, N prune+merge steps, one cross-repo resolution pass, one save — replaces the previous O(K^2) behavior of calling global_add K times. """ tags = tags or [None] * len(graph_paths) if len(tags) != len(graph_paths): raise ValueError("tags must match graph_paths length if provided") global_graph = _load_global_graph() # single load, regardless of K for path, tag in zip(graph_paths, tags): repo_tag = tag or _default_tag(path) repo_graph = _load_repo_graph(path) global_graph = _prune_repo(global_graph, repo_tag) global_graph = _merge_repo(global_graph, repo_graph, repo_tag) global_graph = _resolve_cross_repo(global_graph) # once, after all merges _save_global_graph(global_graph) # single save, regardless of K def global_add(graph_path: Path, tag: str | None = None) -> None: """Back-compat single-repo entry point, now O(1) load/save cost.""" global_add_many([graph_path], [tag]) ``` CLI surface (backwards compatible — single-file form keeps working unchanged): ```text graphify global add [ ...] [--as [ ...]] ``` ### What I still need to verify against the live code before opening the PR - Exact current names/signatures of the load/prune/merge/resolve/save helpers in `global_graph.py` (the snippet above uses placeholder names matching the shape described in this issue — I want to confirm them against `v8` directly rather than assume) - Whether `_prune_repo` + `_merge_repo` are safe to call in a loop as-is, or whether any of the in-place mutation assumptions break when called N times before a single save (e.g. any state that currently resets between calls) - How cross-repo resolution currently gets triggered — confirming it's a separate, callable-once step and not implicitly re-run inside `_merge_repo` ### Test plan - Benchmark test mirroring this issue's 5/10/20/40-repo shape, asserting near-linear rather than quadratic scaling - Equivalence test: `global_add_many([a, b, c])` produces the same graph (nodes/edges/cross-repo links) as three sequential `global_add` calls, on a small fixture set - Existing single-repo `global_add` tests pass unchanged through the new wrapper Will open the PR against this.

I had built and measured one before finding #3434, so rather than sit on it I have opened #3440 and, more usefully, reviewed #3434 against my own numbers. **#3434's core is correct and should probably be the one that lands.** Notably it gets right the thing that is easiest to get wrong: external stubs dedup against what is *already composed*, so the index has to be read off the live graph inside the loop. Hoisting it out of the loop looks like an obvious optimization and silently changes the resulting graph — its comment says exactly this, and it is right.

Three things I found that are worth folding in wherever they land.

### 1. A batch loses the partial-success the loop gave for free

Three graphs, middle one corrupt:

| | result |
|--|--|
| three `global add` calls | A and C land, B fails |
| a batch | **nothing is written** — A and C silently lost |

Both #3434 and my first draft behave the second way. For `graphify global add a.json b.json c.json` that is a regression versus the loop it replaces, and it scales badly. Worth an explicit policy — I used `on_error="abort"` (default) / `"skip"`, exposed as `--keep-going`, with a test that the skip path reproduces the sequential partial-success store exactly.

### 2. The per-unit index rebuild is itself a quadratic term

#3434 rebuilds the external-label index by scanning every node of `G` per unit. Correct, but K whole-graph scans inside the function whose purpose is removing a quadratic term:

| K | node-visits (rebuilt per unit) | (threaded through the loop) |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | 18,027 | 0 |
| 20 | 76,057 | 0 |
| 40 | 312,117 | 0 |
| 80 | 1,264,237 | 0 |

**Being fair to #3434: this does not show up in wall clock at these sizes.** JSON serialization dominates and I measured the two as a wash. Asymptotic cleanup, not a speedup — I would rather say so than oversell it. The fix is to update the index as units contribute stubs instead of rescanning.

### 3. A latent dangling-node bug

Threading the index makes prune-invalidation load-bearing, and testing that surfaced a real defect: when a repo is re-added and its *old* revision owned an external stub, the prune deletes that stub. An index still pointing at it rewires a later unit's edge onto **a node no longer in the graph**. Mutation-tested — disabling invalidation produces exactly that dangling reference. #3434's per-unit rebuild dodges this by accident, but the test is worth having either way.

### Also, pre-existing and easy to hit once batching lands

Tag inference is `source.parent.parent.name`. For `graphify global add /tmp/graph.json` that is the filesystem root — an **empty tag**, which prunes by `""` and registers the repo under a name no later add can address. Harmless-ish today; a batch mixing paths from several layouts makes it much likelier.

### Numbers

400-node units, graphs verified identical to the sequential result at every K:

| K | sequential | batched | speedup |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 | 0.33 s | 0.05 s | 7.3× |
| 10 | 0.73 s | 0.08 s | 8.8× |
| 20 | 2.36 s | 0.27 s | 8.7× |
| 40 | 8.71 s | 0.56 s | 15.5× |

Independently consistent with #3434's 15.2× at K=40, which is reassuring for both.

## Update: adopted @ROHIT8759's rollback, and two notes on the other implementations

@ROHIT8759 has been working the same issue on [`perf/global-add-many`](https://github.com/ROHIT8759/graphify/commits/perf/global-add-many) (no PR opened yet, so it shows on #3438 only as a referenced commit). Their branch went independent → `eaa87c5` (error policies + incremental indexing) → three commits on atomic rollback. Worth reading alongside this one.

### They found something I got wrong

Their rollback work covers a case this PR did not. A unit prunes its repo **before** merging the new revision, so a failure between those two steps leaves the repo removed but not replaced. My `on_error="skip"` had it worse than I realised:

- Only the *source read* was guarded, so a failure in prefix/prune/merge **propagated out of the batch entirely**, ignoring the policy the caller asked for.
- Had it been caught, the batch would then have saved a graph with that repo half-removed.

Fixed in `f8a91d2`, crediting the approach in both the code comment and the commit message. The whole unit is now guarded and a failure restores the repo's nodes and incident edges before the next unit runs, so a skipped unit leaves the store at that repo's previous revision.

Two things I kept from this PR's existing design: nothing is saved when every unit fails, and `abort` still writes nothing at all — so the *store* was never corrupt on this path even before the fix (the half-pruned graph only ever existed in memory and was discarded). The bug was that `skip` didn't skip.

Rollback also must not reintroduce the per-unit whole-graph scan this API exists to remove — the same trap their `a6f675f` had to dig out of. The snapshot is taken only for a repo the loaded graph actually holds nodes for, so adding a new repo pays nothing, and the set of present tags is collected in the same pass that builds the external label index. **A batch still makes exactly one whole-graph scan**, asserted by a test.

Re-measured after the change — no regression: **16.9× over sequential at K=40**, graphs still verified identical to the sequential result at every K. Now 54 tests in `test_global_graph.py`, 196 across related suites.

### Two bugs still open in that branch

Flagging here since there's no PR to review against, and they don't apply to this one:

1. **`cross_repo_calls` is broadcast to every result.** The final loop does `r["cross_repo_calls"] = cross_repo_calls` for each unit, so a 3-repo batch resolving 1 call reports `1, 1, 1` — which reads as 3. The pass runs once over the composed graph and its output doesn't divide over the units that produced it. #3434 and this PR both keep it batch-level only; #3434's test explicitly asserts it is absent from per-unit results.

2. **The store is rewritten even when every unit fails.** Under `skip`, `_save_global_graph` / `_save_manifest` run unconditionally after the loop, so a batch where nothing composed still rewrites the store with an unchanged graph — turning a read failure into a possible write failure. This PR returns early with `saved: False` in that case.

### Where this leaves the three implementations

#3434 (oldest, reviewed), this one, and @ROHIT8759's branch now all implement #3438 — itself a duplicate of #3433. That's a lot of duplicated effort on one fix, and it's a maintainer call to resolve. My position is unchanged from the top of this PR: I'd rather the fix land than that mine does. Happy to reduce this to just the parts the chosen implementation lacks — on current reading that would be the batch-level `cross_repo_calls`, the all-fail early return, the single-scan rollback, and the empty-tag inference fix.

## Review findings addressed — `6a42ff9`

Thanks both. All four of @copilot's findings were real; I verified each against the code before changing anything rather than taking them on faith.

### Fixed

**1. Size cap enforced after hashing.** Correct and it was my own regression — `v8` checked the cap before parsing, and I moved the hash ahead of it. `_file_hash` does `read_bytes()`, so an oversized graph was pulled into memory to compute a hash for a unit about to be rejected for its size. The cap now runs first for every unit, before anything reads the file; under `skip` the cap error is recorded without hashing. Test asserts `_file_hash` is never called when the cap trips.

**2. `--as <tag> <graph.json>` was rejected.** Also correct, and a genuine backward incompatibility — I checked `v8`'s parser and it set `tag` independently of position, so the option-first form worked. Now `--as` tags the *next* graph when it appears before one, and the trailing-graph form still works. A `--as` that would tag nothing is an error rather than silently dropped.

**3. "global graph not modified" per skipped unit.** Untrue in a batch where other units changed it. Now "not re-added", scoped to that repo.

**4. `error` key always present.** Docstring said it appeared only on failures. Documented as it behaves; `global_add`'s single-repo result keeps its original five keys, asserted by a test.

Writing these up exposed that **the CLI half had no test coverage at all** — three of the four are CLI- or shape-level and the Python-level suite could not have caught them. Added `tests/test_cli_global_add_batch.py` (10 tests) driving the real entry point as a subprocess with `HOME`/`USERPROFILE` redirected, since the store path resolves from `Path.home()` at import time.

Now 57 tests in `test_global_graph.py` + 10 CLI, 202 across related suites, lint clean. Re-benchmarked: no regression, graphs still verified identical to the sequential result at every K.

### Not changed, with reasoning

**"`global_add` return shape changed from single-repo result to batch envelope"** (graphify bot, high) — I believe this is a false positive. `global_add` is unchanged: same signature, same five keys, same values. It delegates to `global_add_many` and unwraps `["results"][0]`, and `test_global_add_delegating_result_has_no_error_key` pins the exact key set. The *new* `global_add_many` returns the envelope, but nothing previously called it. The three `cli.py` call sites are untouched. Happy to be shown otherwise if the analysis is seeing a path I'm not.

**"Concurrent `global_add_many` calls can overwrite each other"** and **"graph and manifest writes are not serialized as one transaction"** (high/medium) — both real, both pre-existing on `v8` and unchanged in kind by this PR. Two concurrent `global add`s already raced the same way; batching changes the window's length, not its existence. There is no lock file in the current design, so fixing it properly means introducing one, which is a separate change with its own semantics to settle (blocking vs. failing fast, staleness, cross-platform behaviour) and shouldn't ride along in a perf PR.

On the write ordering specifically, the current order is deliberate and documented in the code: graph first, then manifest. A crash between them leaves nodes the manifest doesn't list, which the next add heals by pruning the tag and recomposing. The reverse strands a recorded hash whose nodes are absent, and every later add then *skips* that repo — a silent permanent hole. I verified the recovery behaviour empirically rather than reasoning about it. Happy to open a follow-up issue for real transactionality if that's wanted.

**Coupling findings** (`global_add_many` fan-out, `global_remove` Ca·Ce, test-helper efferent coupling) — `global_remove` isn't touched by this branch. `global_add_many`'s fan-out is `global_add`'s, relocated: the delegation edge is the point, since one composition implementation means a change to the merge semantics can't land in the batch path and miss the single-unit path. Splitting the body to lower the number would trade a metric for exactly the duplication the delegation prevents. Same conclusion @xiongjianxu reached on #3434, for the same reason.

A third case for the state table in the comment above: **commit identity is the wrong predicate when `graphify-out/` is tracked inside the corpus it indexes.**

Every row of that table compares `built_at_commit` to `HEAD` by ancestry. That holds when the graph lives outside the tree. When `graphify-out/` is committed — the only way the graph shows up in review diffs — the index can never name its own commit: committing the rebuilt graph moves `HEAD` one past the stamp it just wrote. The stamp is therefore *permanently* an ancestor, and that lag is structural rather than evidence of anything.

Concretely, on 0.9.54 with a tracked `graphify-out/` and the convention of a separate reindex commit:

```
stamp = 64f7c15   HEAD = 081e4a5

git rev-parse HEAD                                    → differs  → "stale"
git diff 64f7c15 HEAD -- . ':(exclude)graphify-out'   → empty    → nothing indexed changed
```

Against the table that classifies as `ancestor, ≤ N commits` → `FRESH (report the lag)` — the right verdict for the wrong reason, and it decays. Both commits between those two SHAs touched nothing but `graphify-out/` (a reindex and a label refresh), and a repo whose post-commit hook reindexes routinely accumulates them without bound, pushing the count past any fixed `N` into `STALE` with no source having changed. There is no correct `N`, because the quantity being thresholded is not a measure of staleness.

The fix is to stop asking about commits and ask about content:

```bash
git diff --quiet "$built_at_commit" -- . ":(exclude)${GRAPHIFY_OUT:-graphify-out}"
```

Exit 0 is fresh. Three properties the ancestry check doesn't have:

- **No threshold.** It answers exactly "has any indexed path changed since the build," which is the actual question.
- **It catches uncommitted edits.** Diffing against the working tree rather than a second rev means a dirty tree registers. A `HEAD`-to-`HEAD` comparison misses that entirely — the first comment lists "relevant dirty-worktree changes" as a separate concern, and this collapses it into the same command. Verified both ways: appending a line to a tracked source file flips it to stale, reverting flips it back.
- **It subsumes `DIVERGENT`.** On a divergent branch the diff is non-empty, so it reports stale with no `merge-base` call. Keeping `git merge-base --is-ancestor` is still worthwhile to *name* that state, since divergence wants a full rebuild rather than `--update` — but as a classifier applied after the freshness verdict, not as the verdict itself.

On `GRAPH_REPORT.md` printing the check rather than running it: agreed, and worth noting the printed check carries this same defect, so emitting a verdict fixes both halves at once. I've patched `report.py` locally to emit the source-scoped command instead of the `rev-parse` instruction, which is the shape I'd suggest, but it belongs inside whatever state-machine work lands here rather than as a change of its own.

One caveat against my own suggestion: the exclusion is `graphify-out` by convention and `GRAPHIFY_OUT` by configuration, but a graph written elsewhere via `--out` is covered by neither at report time. Deriving the excluded path from the actual output directory would be more robust than reading the env var.

Reproduced the outward symptom — a plain `import module` + `module.func()` call genuinely produces no `calls` edge — but on current `main` (`91f4d12`) none of the functions/mechanism cited here (`_file_node_id`, `_repoint_python_package_imports`, `_resolve_python_member_calls`, `contains_children`, `symbol_resolution.py`) exist. I couldn't find any of them anywhere in the tree, so I want to share what I actually found before anyone builds against the description above.

**What `extract_python` (`graphify/extract.py`) actually does today:**

- File-level ids are *always* the bare stem (`_make_id(stem)`, extract.py:64) — there is no directory-prefixed id anywhere, so the "`scripts_greeter` vs `greeter`" id-mismatch this issue describes doesn't apply. I confirmed this directly: on your exact two-file repro, `main.py`'s `imports` edge target (`greeter`) and `greeter.py`'s real file-node id (`greeter`) are identical strings — no dangling id.
- The actual reason no `calls` edge appears: the call-graph pass (extract.py:152-198) builds `label_to_nid` purely from the nodes collected while walking *this one file* (see the `nodes` list built during `walk(root)` a few lines above it). `extract_python` is invoked once per file with no cross-file context, so `say_hello` is simply never in `main.py`'s own `label_to_nid` — it's not an id-mismatch, there's no cross-file call resolution at all for attribute-style calls, regardless of directory layout or `__init__.py` presence.
- This is a different limitation than `_resolve_cross_file_imports` (extract.py:2123), which does have cross-file logic, but only for `from .module import Name` → it emits `uses` edges from same-file *classes* to the imported name, and never looks at call expressions. Plain `import module` (no `from`) isn't part of that pass, and neither `from`- nor plain-`import` attribute calls get a `calls` edge produced anywhere.

Repro (ran against current `main`, tree-sitter-python installed locally):
```
greeter.py nodes: ['greeter', 'greeter_say_hello']
main.py nodes: ['main', 'main_run']
main.py edges: [imports main->greeter, contains main->main_run]
```
No `calls` edge, as you described — just not for the id-mismatch reason.

**Proposed direction**, scoped to what's actually here: extend `_resolve_cross_file_imports`'s two-pass shape (or add a sibling pass reusing its `stem_to_entities` map) to also index top-level *functions*, not just classes, and to handle plain `import module` targets (matching `attribute` call nodes like `module.func()` against `stem_to_entities[module]`), the same way it currently matches `from module import func` names against local classes. That reuses the existing merge point in the pipeline that already has all per-file results in hand, rather than trying to make single-file `extract_python` calls aware of each other.

One question on `{closure@<line>}`. Node ids appear to derive from labels, so a line number in the label puts a line number in the id. That means any edit above a closure renames every closure below it, and an incremental `update` evicts and recreates those nodes rather than matching them. Saved community labels and anything citing a closure id would go stale on an unrelated edit. The test hard-coding `{closure@2}` / `{closure@5}` shows the coupling.

Two alternatives that keep ids stable across edits:

1. **Ordinal within the enclosing scope** — `{closure#1}`, `{closure#2}` within a file or function. Stable unless closures are added or reordered, which is a much rarer edit than adding a line above one.
2. **Derive from the call it is passed to** — for the routing case this is both stable and more useful. `$app->get('/api', function () {})` becomes something like `GET /api`, which is what someone querying the graph would actually search for. This is the case the issue was filed about, so it may be worth special-casing the argument position even if unnamed closures elsewhere keep a generic name.

Separately, adding the closure types to `function_boundary_types` means calls inside a closure now attribute to the closure instead of the enclosing named function. That is probably the correct behaviour, but it moves existing edges on any codebase that already has closures inside named functions, so it may deserve a changelog note.

## Correction pushed: the PHP resolver was rewriting other languages' import edges

An adversarial review of this branch rejected it, and it was right. `38e6e67` fixes it.

### The defect

`metadata.target_fqn` is a shared metadata key. C# `using` directives and other language extractors stamp it as well. `_resolve_php_type_references` is handed every edge in the graph, not only PHP ones, so the per-edge lookup this branch added was consuming other languages' values.

The check has to run *before* the `ref_file not in ns_by_file` gate, because emptying that map is exactly what the multi-namespace bailout does and that bailout is the bug being fixed. Hoisting it above the gate also hoisted it out of the only thing that had been scoping this function to PHP.

Measured, in a scan containing one namespaced PHP file plus `Use.kt` with `import external.lib.Widget`:

| revision | Kotlin import target | node materialised |
|---|---|---|
| `v8` | `widget` | none |
| this branch before `38e6e67` | `external_lib_widget` | `external.lib.Widget` |
| this branch after `38e6e67` | `widget` | none |

C# `using` directives were rebindable the same way.

### The fix

Provenance is now required explicitly rather than inherited from control flow. `_is_php_source` mirrors the suffix set `extract.py` already selects PHP files on, including its `.blade.php` exclusion, and the FQN is consumed only for an edge a PHP file produced. The multi-namespace behaviour this branch exists to fix is untouched, since it never depended on the gate the check sits above.

### Verification

```
python -m pytest tests/test_php_type_resolution.py -q
23 passed
```

Deleting the single `_is_php_source(ref_file)` clause turns `test_php_import_identity_does_not_touch_other_languages` red and leaves the other 22 green, so the guard is load-bearing rather than decorative.

Full suite on the branch head: 5499 passed, 13 skipped. `ruff` and `py_compile` clean.

Worth noting for reviewers: CI was green on the previous head and the pull request was marked mergeable throughout. A cross-language rebind that no existing test covers is invisible to the suite, which is why this needed a separate pass rather than a re-run.

A data point for why this matters beyond lineage, from a codebase that keeps every query in its
own `.sql` file (loaded by name from a single loader module, ~220 statement files plus ~50
migrations).

With `tree-sitter-sql` installed, `extract_sql` produced 312 nodes — but **259 of the 270 `.sql`

edges); the statement files yield a bare file node, because a file whose entire content is a
`SELECT` / `UPDATE` / `INSERT` has no `create_*` node for the walker to hit. In a
SQL-in-files layout that is the majority of the corpus, so the language looks extracted while
the part carrying the actual contracts is inert.

Table references from DML — the lineage this issue proposes — is exactly what would connect
them: each statement node gaining edges to the tables it reads and writes would take those 259
isolated nodes into the graph proper.

For what it is worth, the caller-side half is recoverable outside graphify: scanning the loader
module's `key: load('file.sql')` map and the `SQL.<key>` call sites gave 586 statement↔caller
edges deterministically, no grammar needed. It is the *inside* of the statement — which tables
and columns it touches — that only a parser can supply, which is the gap here.

Checked this against current `main` (`91f4d12`) and the driver script in the repro doesn't match the current API, so I want to flag that before anyone tries to reproduce this as written.

`graphify.extract.extract()` (extract.py:2256) has signature `extract(paths: list[Path]) -> dict` — no `cache_root` or `parallel` keyword arguments exist. Calling it as `extract(files, cache_root=root, parallel=False)`, as the repro script does, raises `TypeError: extract() got an unexpected keyword argument 'cache_root'` on current source. `root` for cache purposes is computed internally from the common path prefix of the given `paths` (extract.py:2266-2279), not passed in.

Separately, the per-file cache (`graphify/cache.py`) is keyed purely by **SHA256 of file contents** (`file_hash`, cache.py:9-11), not by path — `cache_dir(root)` only decides *where* the cache directory lives (`Path(root).resolve() / "graphify-out" / "cache"`, cache.py:16), it doesn't factor into the cache *key*. So identical file content scanned via a symlinked vs. real root would hit the exact same cache entries either way; a symlink-dependent edge-count difference can't come from the cache layer as it exists today.

More fundamentally, I don't see a code path that would produce a `calls` edge for a cross-file constructor call (`Settings()` invoked from a different file than where `Settings` is defined) at all, symlink or not — `_resolve_cross_file_imports` (extract.py:2123, the only cross-file pass for Python) only ever emits `relation: "uses"` edges from classes to `from X import Y` targets; it never emits `"calls"`. So I can't get the reported baseline (`calls` edges present under the real path) to make sense against current source, independent of the symlink question.

## Workaround for anyone hitting this before it lands upstream

Posting what we run, since both this and the sibling issue bite the same repos and the fix is the same shape either way.

We do **not** patch the installed package — `uv tool upgrade` silently reverts it, and a workaround that disappears on upgrade is worse than none. Instead we re-derive the missing edges from source and inject them into `graph.json` as a build step.

### Where it goes in the pipeline

```
graphify extract . --code-only
  └─ graph-repair.py graph.json      <-- inject here
graphify cluster-only . --no-label --no-viz
```

**Before `cluster-only`, deliberately.** Communities, the god-node ranking and the cycle list in `GRAPH_REPORT.md` are then all computed from the repaired graph rather than one missing a sixth of its imports.

### What gets written

One `imports_from` link per recovered file pair, between the two files' `L1` nodes — the shape graphify already uses for a file-to-file dependency:

```python
{"source": file_node[src], "target": file_node[dst],
 "relation": "imports_from", "_origin": "graph-repair",
 "confidence": "EXTRACTED", "confidence_score": 1.0,
 "context": "import", "source_file": src, "source_location": "L1", "weight": 1.0}
```

The `_origin` tag matters: injected edges stay greppable and never pass as graphify's own extraction.

Result — `graphify explain` sees an edge it could not resolve itself:

```
$ graphify explain "sign-in-magic-link.tsx"
Connections (3):
  <-- auth/actions.ts [imports_from] [EXTRACTED]  packages/services/src/auth/actions.ts:L1
```

### Four things that cost us a debugging cycle each

**1. A top-level marker does not survive.** Setting `graph["import_repair"] = {...}` is dropped by `cluster-only`, which keeps only keys it writes itself — `built_at_commit` survives because graphify sets it, a custom key does not. Per-link attributes *do* survive, so detection has to be "are there links with my `_origin`", not a header field.

**2. Strip your previous injection BEFORE computing what already exists.** Otherwise run two sees last run's edges, treats every candidate as already present, skips them all, then deletes them — leaving the graph worse than unrepaired, and only ever on the second run. Order:

```python
links = [l for l in links if l.get("_origin") != ORIGIN]   # strip first
existing = {(path(l["source"]), path(l["target"])) for l in links if ...}
```

**3. `graphify update` rewrites `graph.json` and drops the injection.** So the step has to run on *every* command that writes the file, not once by hand. Ours is wired into the build / clean / update wrapper and is idempotent, so re-running recovers.

**4. Do not also repair on read.** We first had our downstream consumers re-derive the same edges when loading `graph.json`. Once the file itself was repaired that double-counted every pair graphify had partially resolved, and inflated our package-level edge weights by 10-20%. Repair in one place; have readers warn if the marker is missing rather than silently re-deriving.

### Scope

The resolver handles relative specifiers (`./Foo.js` → `Foo.ts` / `Foo.tsx` / `Foo.d.ts`, plus `Foo.native.tsx` / `Foo.web.tsx` for bundler platform splits) and workspace subpaths through `exports` maps, choosing the export condition by the importing file's platform. ~540 edges on a 1,430-file monorepo.

Happy to contribute the resolution logic as a PR against `_resolve_js_import_path` if that is wanted — it is the same matching, just inside graphify instead of bolted on after.

Thanks for the review.

**"Symlink-loop .graphify_root can crash generated hooks" — confirmed and fixed.** Reproduced directly: `Path.resolve()` raises `RuntimeError` for a symlink loop, not `OSError`, so the guard's `except OSError` let it propagate. It doesn't produce a raw traceback (the outer `except Exception` in the hook body catches it and reports "Rebuild failed"), but that's still wrong — a bad marker should fall back to the repo top like every other invalid value, not abort the rebuild. Fixed in the latest commit by also catching `RuntimeError`, with a regression test that builds an actual two-symlink loop and confirms the fallback now fires.

**"Checkout hook validated path is reopened after symlink race" — looked at this, leaving it as is.** This is a TOCTOU between the `resolve()` check and `_rebuild_code`'s actual use of `_root` a few lines later. I don't think it changes the threat model this PR is closing: the scenario #3265 describes (and what this guard defends against) is a value committed to the repo steering a later, unattended run of the hook. A TOCTOU exploit needs an attacker with live, precisely-timed write access to the working tree *during* the hook's execution window on the victim's own machine — at that point they already have a much more direct path to doing damage than racing a path check (they could edit the source files being rebuilt, or the hook script itself). Happy to revisit if there's a concrete scenario where that access exists without also implying worse compromise already, but I don't think a file-descriptor-based rewrite of `_rebuild_code`'s read/write path is proportionate to add here.

Measured on 0.9.57 with the same routing gap, from the other end: the heading nodes are not only skipped in the skill path, they are also skipped by headless `graphify extract --backend claude-cli`, and a later `graphify update` does not bring them back.

### Setup

One TypeScript/JavaScript monorepo, 910 code files, 18 markdown files, 44 documents total for the semantic tier, built four ways from the same commit, all with `diagnose multigraph` clean (0 dangling, 0 duplicate, 0 self-loop).

| Build | markdown nodes | semantic edges | a README section node findable by `query`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `graphify update` (AST only) | 238 (file + heading nodes) | 0 | yes |
| `graphify extract --backend claude-cli` | 18 (one `_doc` node per file) | 44 | **no** |
| the above, then `graphify update` | 18 | 44 | no |
| skill Part A run over code **and** `.md`, then Part C merge with the semantic tier, `build_from_json` | 238 | 43 | yes |

### Reading of the code

`detect` classifies `.md` as `document`; the backend path hands documents to the semantic tier and never calls `extract_markdown`, and the skill's Part A passes only `detect['files']['code']` to `extract()` (this issue). After a semantic layer exists, the #2014 / #1915 guards keep `update` from quick-scanning the file, so the headings stay absent. `_doc_twin_remap` (#1799) handles the file-node twin only.

### Why the headings matter to a reader

A heading node is a pointer to a section, with a line. In a review workflow "does a document already cover X" is answered by that pointer and then by reading the file. The `_doc` node carries a good summary, but `query` no longer lands on the section, so the answer degrades from "README L159, this heading" to "some README".

### What worked

Running `extract()` over the `.md` files as well as code, and merging the semantic tier on top in Part C, keeps both: the heading nodes and their `contains` structure from `extract_markdown`, plus the `_doc` node and its semantic edges for the same file. `build_from_json` accepted the mix without collisions. If that is an acceptable shape, the fix on the skill side is a one-line change to Part A's file selection; the CLI side would need the backend path to run the structural markdown pass before the semantic one.

Thanks for the review. Went through all four findings.

**"Fallback does not preserve os.replace semantics for symlink destinations" and "Fallback replace follows destination symlinks" — both real, confirmed and fixed.** Reproduced directly: `os.replace` on a symlinked destination replaces the link itself (the link's old target is left untouched), while a naive `shutil.copy2(src, dst)` opens `dst` for writing and follows the link, overwriting whatever it points at instead. `install.py`'s own docstring for the version-stamp write explicitly documents relying on the replace-not-follow behavior for managed skill symlinks (#3286), so this would have been a real regression the first time the fallback fired on a symlinked install. Fixed by copying to a fresh temp file beside the destination first, then swapping the destination out from under it via unlink + rename — this replicates `os.replace`'s "whatever was there is gone" semantics regardless of whether a symlink or a regular file was there. Added a regression test that reproduces the exact scenario (a symlinked destination pointing at a separate shared file) and asserts the shared target is untouched.

**"Windows fallback exposes non-atomic partial writes to readers" — this was already true of the pre-existing WinError 5/32 fallback (in `paths.py` and `cache.py`), and my PR extended it to more call sites rather than introducing it.** That said, the redesign above happens to improve this too: copying to a temp file first and only swapping it into place via unlink+rename means the window a reader could observe a half-written destination shrinks from "however long the copy takes" to two back-to-back metadata operations, for every covered call site now, not just the ones that already had a fallback.

**"copy2 fallback fails on directory replace (WinError 17 for dirs)" — not reachable today.** `os_replace_with_fallback` is only ever called with individual files across this PR's 7 touched call sites (SKILL.md, version stamp, cache entries, stat index, GraphML) — the one directory-level `os.replace` in `install.py` (the `references/` sidecar swap) was deliberately left on the raw call, exactly because `shutil.copy2`/this fallback don't handle directories. Not currently a live bug, but a fair API-robustness point if that helper is ever reused for a directory swap later; happy to add an explicit `assert not os.path.isdir(src)` guard if you'd like that documented in code rather than just in this reply.

Thanks for the second pass.

**"tempfile module used but not imported in paths.py fallback" — false positive.** `tempfile` is imported at module level (`graphify/paths.py:23`, part of the pre-existing imports this file already had) and used at `tempfile.mkstemp` a few lines above the flagged line; nothing to fix here.

**The other three ("Fallback replace can delete the original file on rename failure", "os_replace_with_fallback deletes source on copy failure via unlink(src)", "Fallback can delete the existing destination if the final rename fails", "Fallback replace exposes a missing-destination window") were all the same real gap, and a fair one to flag at high severity.** The previous version removed whatever sat at the destination and then renamed the new content into place as two separate steps; if the second step failed for any reason, the destination was left missing entirely — worse than the write it was trying to work around. Reproduced directly (forced the final rename to fail) and confirmed the destination ended up gone.

Fixed in the latest commit: instead of unlinking the destination outright, it's renamed aside to a backup path first, and if the final rename-into-place then fails, the backup is renamed straight back before the exception propagates. A plain rename moves a symlink itself rather than following it, so this also keeps the symlink-safety property from the previous round intact. Added a test that forces the final rename to fail and confirms the destination is restored to its original content with no leftover temp files.

(The `unlink(src)` at the very end only runs after the swap has already landed successfully, so a copy or swap failure never reaches it — `src` and `dst` are both left in a defined state either way.)

Third pass, went through all five.

**"Fallback deletes destination when src and dst are the same path" — real, confirmed, fixed.** Reproduced directly: `os_replace_with_fallback(p, p)` crashed with `FileNotFoundError` on the final `unlink(src)`, because the "back dst up by renaming it aside" step moves `src` out from under itself the moment they're the same path. Not reachable through any of this PR's actual call sites (every one passes a distinct freshly-created temp file as `src`), but cheap to guard against directly, so I added an early same-path check that no-ops instead of attempting a swap. Test added.

**"Symlink dst is replaced with a copy of the symlink target's content, not a plain file" and "...semantics change for symlinked src" — not reachable, and I don't think worth hardening speculatively.** Both describe the same case: `shutil.copy2` dereferences a symlinked *source*, so if `src` itself were ever a symlink, the fallback would land a regular file with the target's content at `dst` instead of preserving `src` as a symlink the way a true `os.replace` would. Checked all 7 call sites this PR touches (`paths.py`, `cache.py` x2, `export.py`, `install.py` x3) — every one passes a plain temp file it just created as `src`, never a symlink. Happy to add `os.readlink` + `os.symlink` handling for a symlinked source if this helper ever grows a caller that needs it, but adding untested complexity for a case nothing currently exercises seems like the wrong trade here.

**"Fallback replace exposes a missing destination window" and "...fallback is non-atomic: dst missing between backup rename and copy rename" — real, and inherent to any fallback for this bug, not something further fixable.** There genuinely is a brief window between the backup rename and the landing rename where `dst` doesn't exist — a concurrent reader hitting that exact instant would see it missing. This can't be closed without an atomic swap primitive, which is precisely what's broken on the affected systems (that's why `os.replace` itself failed and got us here in the first place). What the last round's fix did address is the *failure* case: if the landing rename doesn't succeed, the backup goes straight back rather than leaving `dst` permanently missing. The window on the success path is now two back-to-back rename syscalls rather than however long the copy takes, which is the best available without a working atomic operation — already documented in the docstring, but happy to call it out more explicitly there if useful.

Thanks for this — the review earned its keep. All four distinct findings are real, and three of them I could reproduce against a live graph before touching a word of the text. Fixed in `a9b253d`, force-pushed over `7992600`.

### 1. Single shared state file for every re-extracted document (`…/update.md:84`, and the same finding on the `amp` variant)

Real, and the worst of the four, because it is the one that fails **open**. `.graphify_must_ids.txt` was a fixed path, so in a delta with two changed docs the second snapshot overwrote the first, and that doc went through the merge ungated while the gate still printed `GATE: PASS` — a silent hole in the one procedure whose whole job is to fail closed. Reproduced on a 3,545-node graph: snapshot doc A (2 mandatory IDs), snapshot doc B (27), and A's IDs are simply gone from disk.

One clarification on the framing, because it changes what the fix has to be: this isn't a concurrency race. Nothing writes these files concurrently — the extraction subagents write `CHUNK_PATH`, while the snapshot and the gate both run in the host session, sequentially. It is a plain sequential overwrite, which is why keying the state file by target is sufficient and no locking is needed.

**Fix:** state files are keyed by target (`.graphify_must_<slug>.json`), with a one-time clear of stale snapshots before the first target of a run.

### 2 + 3. Suffix collisions from `endswith(TARGET)` (`…:86` and `…:87`)

Real — and the sharpest of the three to demonstrate, because it needs no operator error at all. `endswith` is not anchored to a path boundary, so a `source_file` that is a bare root-level name is a suffix of every same-named file deeper in the tree. On one of our real corpora, `TARGET = 'README.md'` — which is exactly how the root README appears in `source_file`, so there is nothing to mistype — also matched `workers/README.md`:

```
gate (endswith) baseline : 22 nodes
true (exact)   baseline :  7 nodes
FOREIGN nodes pulled in  : 15  (from workers/README.md)
```

The consequence is a hard FAIL on correct output: a *perfect* re-extraction of `README.md` lands at 31.8% of the inflated baseline with 15 mandatory IDs reported missing. And the remedy the procedure then prescribes makes it worse — "re-dispatch naming the missing IDs" tells the subagent to emit another file's nodes under this file's `source_file`, which replace-on-re-extract would then attribute to the wrong file.

**Fix:** match `source_file` exactly. Where no exact match exists but suffix candidates do, the snapshot prints the candidates and stops rather than guessing.

### 4. Gate reads only `.graphify_chunk_01.json` (`…:105`)

Real. One correction to the mechanism, because it shaped the fix: a document never splits across chunks. Step 3B chunks by *file* — 20–25 files per chunk, and each image gets its own — so one file always lands in exactly one chunk. Multiple chunks come from a delta with many semantic files, and then the target doc can sit in `_02` while the gate reads `_01`, sees none of its mandatory IDs, and fails a clean extraction. Not hypothetical: a recent `--update` on our side dispatched two doc subagents on a 14-file delta.

**Fix:** the gate now unions every `.graphify_chunk_*.json` and evaluates every snapshot in one pass. That also closed a latent over-count nobody flagged — the old `len(d['nodes'])` was the whole chunk, so for any chunk holding more than one file the 90% shrink check was measured against the wrong number. It now counts only the nodes attributed to each target, longest-suffix wins, so `workers/README.md` nodes are not counted against `README.md`.

### Verification

Two-chunk delta with the target in `_02` now passes with correct per-doc counts (7/7 and 15/15), and two negative controls confirm the gate can still fail: drop one mandatory node → `FAIL` with the ID named; drop one baseline hyperedge → `FAIL`. All five skillgen guards pass. `pytest tests/` is 5412 passed / 95 skipped — the only failures are the four `test_ollama_retry_cap.py` tests that need the uninstalled `openai` extra and reproduce identically on a pristine checkout, plus one `scales_linearly` timing test that passes in isolation.

Worth saying plainly: this gate text runs in production for us, across a six-project fleet, in a hardened superset of this fragment. So these are not edits to a proposal — the identical three fixes went into the live copy in the same pass, which is also where the reproductions above came from.

CI is showing `action_required` on the new SHA, so it is waiting on a workflow approval whenever that is convenient. No rush on any of it, and as before I am happy to reshape the whole thing if a lighter touch would suit the project better.

Thanks — worked through all three, and rebased onto v8 (0.9.59):

**Shadowing test (real, fixed in f263ab2).** Correct catch: the old test declared a *differently-named* local (`T2`), so it never shadowed anything, and `edges == [] or ...` passed vacuously. Rewritten as a parameter `Thing T` shadowed by an inner-block local `Other T`, asserting the call binds to `Other::Ready` — which resolves only if the local wins the fold; a params-first regression leaves `Thing` (no `Ready`) and yields no edge. Decisive now, no empty-set escape.

**File-wide table / field-vs-local ordering (pre-existing conservative design, not a regression).** The `var -> ClassName` table has been file-scoped and first-write-wins since #1547 (`_cpp_local_var_types`); this PR folds parameters and fields into that same table in lookup order (local → parameter → field), documented at the call site. It's deliberately conservative: a same-named receiver in an unrelated scope can bind to the first-seen type, but that only ever costs a *missed* edge, never a false one — the corpus resolver emits an edge solely when the receiver type resolves to exactly one definition AND that type actually declares the method (`method_index[(type_nid, method_key)]`). A wrong-type binding fails the method-exists check and is dropped. Per-body scoping would add marginal recall at the cost of reworking the shared #1547 machinery and the file-keyed resolver lookup, so I've kept this PR scoped to the parameter/field gap it set out to close. Happy to file a follow-up for true per-scope typing if that recall is wanted.

Worked through all three (rebased onto 0.9.59):

**Pool abort waited for running workers (real, fixed).** Correct — although the handler calls `shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)`, it re-raises out of the `with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool` block, so the executor's `__exit__` then calls `shutdown(wait=True)` and blocks on the other in-flight workers — each potentially churning the memory the budget just tripped on, the opposite of a prompt abort. The handler now terminates the live workers before re-raising, so the implicit exit-shutdown finds them gone and returns at once.

**Flag races through process-global environment.** `_arm_memory_budget` runs once at CLI dispatch in the main process, before any pool exists; writing `GRAPHIFY_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB` to the environment is the intended mechanism for the spawn-based workers (and nested rebuilds) to inherit the cap — spawn workers don't inherit Python globals, only the environment. There's no concurrent second extract in the same process to race it. Left as-is by design.

**ThreadPool substitution runs the initializer in the pytest process.** Fair observation about the harness: the thread-pool substitution exercises the budget-application and abort-propagation logic without spawning real subprocesses (so it runs deterministically in CI), which is deliberate — the process-pool path itself is covered by the worker-init and BrokenProcessPool tests. Both review passes checked by execution; here is what each finding turned out to be and what changed.

**Round 1 — "Alias-qualified generic extension receivers are dropped" (engine.py:2820)** — real; fixed in dbe0936. `extension<T>(Alias::IFoo<T> spec)` / `global::IFoo<T>` produced no `references` and no `calls` edge because the ERROR-shape text path did not treat `::` as a qualifier separator. The shared node helpers had the same gap, pre-existing and wider: with no `alias_qualified_name` branch, `global::IFoo` in *any* type position (field, base list, primary-constructor parameter) fabricated a phantom `global` type node and bound the receiver to it, and the dotted `global::Acme.IFoo` carried `global::Acme` as its qualifier, which no namespace matches, so the reference was repointed to a dangling stub.

**Round 2 — #1 and #3, "split on dots inside generic arguments" (engine.py:222, :3104)** — real, and pre-existing in `v8`: the qualified branch ran `rpartition(".")` over the whole node text, so `Acme.IFoo<System.String>` as a field or base type became a phantom `String>` qualified by `Acme.IFoo<System` (reproduced on `v8` head, before this PR), and `Outer<int>.Inner` carried `Outer<int>` as its qualifier. Fixed in 3080deb.

**Fix for all of the above** — one normaliser, `_csharp_dotted_name`: drop every `<…>` list (nesting included) and fold the alias qualifier (`global::` → root, which every scope list already contains; `X::B` → `X.B`, which `resolve_qualified` already handles), *then* split. Used by `_read_csharp_type_name`, `_csharp_collect_type_refs`, and the receiver text path, so every C# type reference reads a name the same way. Identity on text with neither `<` nor `::`.

**Round 2 — #2, "`qualified=False` for `global::` names changes the resolver contract"** — no existing emission changed. A `qualified_name` node always has a top-level dot, so its prefix is non-empty and it still emits `qualified=True`; the only `qualified=False` case is the undotted `alias_qualified_name` (`global::IFoo`), which the helpers previously did not handle at all (it fell into child recursion and emitted *two* unqualified refs, `global` and `IFoo`). Resolving it through the scope list is also safe: the root namespace is in every scope list, and `resolve_type_name` binds only when exactly one candidate exists, so a same-named type in another in-scope namespace yields no edge rather than a wrong one. Emitting `qualified=True` with an empty qualifier would instead make `resolve_qualified` return `None` and repoint to a dangling stub.

**Tests** — 10 added across the two commits (both block shapes × `global::Acme.IFoo` / `Alias::IFoo` resolve to the real `Acme.IFoo` node, not a stub; root-anchored receiver is unqualified; the primary-constructor path no longer fabricates `global`; dotted generic arguments on a receiver, a field, and a base list; `Outer<int>.Inner`). Each fails on the commit before its fix. Full suite, ruff, and pyright unchanged from `v8`.

**Coupling notes** — answered inline: `_csharp_collect_type_refs` gains one callee and its fan-in is the number of C# type positions; `_csharp_extension_blocks` fans out to the existing primitives so three parse shapes share one receiver rule; the test helper is the shared contract. The "new hotspots" list (`_extract_generic`, `extract_js`, `extract_xaml`, …) names pre-existing functions the diff neither adds nor edits.

Investigated this against current `v8` HEAD (this issue was filed against `graphifyy 0.8.14`, quite old) and all three reported symptoms are already fixed.

**Root cause 1 (raw string comparison, absolute vs relative)** — fixed. `build_merge`/`merge_raw_extraction` no longer compare `prune_sources` against `source_file` with plain string equality; `_build_prune_sets` (`graphify/build.py:461`) builds match sets covering the raw form, the root-relativized form (`_norm_source_file`), and a form-independent absolute identity (`_abs_identity`) for every prune entry, checked in that order by `_prune_match`.

**Root cause 2 (case mismatch between `.graphify_root` and the real filesystem case, macOS/Windows)** — also already handled, though not by case-folding directly. Reproduced the exact scenario: a graph built under the real-case path, then `build_merge` called with `root=` holding a different-case root than the deleted file's absolute path. `_abs_identity`/`.resolve()` indeed does not case-fold (confirmed directly — Python's `Path.resolve()` is not case-normalizing even on a case-insensitive filesystem), so the direct match with the wrong root fails as the issue describes. But when that happens, `_derive_prune_root` (#2446, `build.py:498`) kicks in: it derives the correct root by suffix-matching the absolute prune path's *tail* against the graph's own stored relative `source_file` — a plain string operation that's naturally case-exact and doesn't depend on the (possibly wrong-case) root at all — then re-runs the prune with the derived root. In my repro this correctly pruned the node despite the case mismatch.

**Root cause 3 (misleading "already clean" message)** — also fixed. `build.py:2119-2149`: when prune entries exist but truly matched nothing (including after the derive-root fallback above also failed), the code now prints a `WARNING: N prune source(s) matched no nodes or edges` with a concrete example of the mismatched entry and a stored `source_file` for comparison — not "already clean". The "already clean" message is now reached only when `prune_sources` was empty to begin with.

Ran the issue's own exact repro verbatim (arbitrary absolute prefix, no `root=` passed at all) against current `v8`:

assert 'the_node_id' not in G   # PASSES on current v8
